heading: Networks trained from different seeds can share features and subspaces
definition: networks of the same architecture trained from different initializations learn many of the same features or shared subspaces, though not the same individual units or bases.
summary: Several studies find shared features or similar representation geometry across seeds, but broad convergence is contested and depends on layer, task and comparison method. Some CNN, BERT and toy Transformer comparisons show weak or no correspondence, while evidence that CNNs favor the coordinate axes defined by their units weakens claims that models cannot share units or bases.

suggested_status.by_scale: Toy: conditional support, with independent-reproduction level unresolved (?), plus a reviewed challenge (C) for concrete key representations in specific group-composition Transformer seeds (arXiv:2302.03025); <1B: conditional support, with independent-reproduction level unresolved (?); 1–10B: ? for independently initialized base models, since explicit coverage concerns fixed-model SAE fitting; 10–100B and >100B: ? with no explicit coverage. Size-unstated CNN comparisons include a reviewed challenge (C); an English BERT seed comparison whose size the pack does not state has a single-layer challenge (C) under paraphrase inputs (arXiv:1911.01464).
suggested_status.reason: The literal version is contested by reviewed activation-subspace results reporting very low intermediate CNN matching (arXiv:1810.11750#r1), while aligned-geometry evidence supports a narrower conditional claim (arXiv:1811.11684#r2,#r3). Preferred native CNN bases also qualify the categorical basis exclusion (arXiv:2502.18710#R5–R8). The checks added two condition-specific challenges. English BERT seed models have layer-7 CKA 0.24 versus 0.32 for a random-target-encoder control, on paraphrase rather than identical inputs (arXiv:1911.01464#r1). C113 Transformer seeds 2 and 4 and A5 Transformer seed 4 share no key representations with the other Transformer seeds on the same group, in toy group-composition tasks where a common circuit family recurs (arXiv:2302.03025#R30,#R32,#R56). Neither of these two studies shares authors with an original. Another challenge is informal and performance-confounded (lw:uTPetRBbkP4p6FhGf#r10). counts: versions.V3.verdicts.challenges.studies=2, versions.V3.verdicts.supports.studies=79 and versions.V3.studies_with_limits_scope=48. These counts predate the checker's corrections. The challenges count covers only arXiv:1810.11750 and lw:uTPetRBbkP4p6FhGf; it excludes arXiv:1911.01464 and arXiv:2302.03025, whose pre-check V3 verdicts were supports and limits_scope, and limits_scope only. These counts describe verdict coverage, not independent replications. versions.V3.studies_by_size lacks 10-100B and >100B; headers do not establish study-specific author independence well enough to assign reliable per-scale R2 levels.
suggested_status.open_questions: A matched comparison of activation-subspace matching, CKA and held-out functional transfer on the same well-performing seed pairs would clarify the CNN challenge. Identical inside-block stitch grids and training recipes would test the ResNet-18 conflict. An identical-input English BERT seed comparison would show whether the layer-7 result below the random-target-encoder control persists without paraphrase inputs. Group-composition comparisons beyond toy Transformers would show whether absent key-representation recurrence in some seeds extends past the tested settings. Explicit author provenance, independently trained 1–10B and larger base-model replicas, and instruction/chat or reasoning-stage comparisons would change the scale-specific assessment. A complete causal feature inventory would clarify how much structure is shared beyond reconstruction and metric summaries.

source.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
source.authors: Yi-Xuan Li; J. Yosinski; J. Clune; Hod Lipson; J. Hopcroft

original_result.setup: The study compared two networks, Net1 and Net2, by matching units, fitting linear maps with few nonzero weights, and clustering similar features.
original_result.result: Shared features in the first convolutional layer (conv1) included Gabor filters, edge orientations and color blobs, but 17% of conv1 units and 92% of fourth-layer (conv4) units had no partner with correlation above 0.5. A sparse conv1 map used 4.7 source units per target unit and had loss 0.235, compared with 0.170 for a dense map, which allows every source unit to contribute.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Word embeddings shared substantial subspaces across seeds, though individual dimensions matched poorly.
Networks shared aligned representation directions across seeds, and small shared subspaces preserved accuracy.
Representations converged across seeds, especially in early layers and wider networks.
ConvNets developed shared representational geometry during training despite different arrangements of individual feature axes.
After linear alignment, seeds arranged nearby samples almost identically, with low error on the fitting data.
VAE seeds selected for high agreement with other seeds recovered similar interpretable factors.
Differential-equation networks reproduced early representations across seeds, with greater reproducibility at larger widths.
English language models shared early-layer representations across seeds more than untrained random encoders did.
CIFAR-10 networks shared substantial linear subspaces across seeds, especially in deeper architectures.
Navigation agents learned similar but distinct visual subspaces across seeds.
Neuron matching revealed subsets of highly correlated features across independently trained classifiers.
Student networks wider than their teachers repeatedly specialized in the same teacher features across seeds.
Reinforcement-learning Q-network ensembles whose training targets depended on one another learned highly similar representations across seeds.
MNIST MLPs shared many matching neurons and correlated representation directions across random initializations.
Reordering neurons recovered moderate feature correspondence between independently trained ResNet-56 models.
Corresponding BERT layers were closer across seeds than selected layers within a model.
ResNet50 models shared substantial representation structure across seeds, yet each retained information the others lacked.
CIFAR representations scored highly on CKA similarity and rarely disagreed on downstream predictions.
Music CNNs learned highly similar but distinct convolutional representations across initializations.
Joining models' layers through linear maps preserved CIFAR-10 performance at every tested layer across independent seeds.
The GULP similarity measure revealed convergence across ResNet18 seeds and shared later-layer structure in BERT.
Independent ResNet50 models shared some nearly identical first-layer filters after matching.
CNN representations aligned through linear maps plus offsets; restricting matches to few units reduced accuracy.
Myrtle CNN seeds shared representations alignable by linear maps beyond simply reordering neurons.
Activation matching enabled network averaging with little or no accuracy barrier in tested settings.
Independently initialized BERT models developed highly similar representational geometry.
VGG11 seeds learned first-layer filters with highly consistent distributions of energy across frequencies.
Autoencoder seeds preserved angles between latent points, enabling effective encoder–decoder swaps using relative representations.
Accurate recurrent networks converged to nearly identical circuit spectra across seeds.
Activation matching enabled VGG11 seed pairs to merge with modest accuracy barriers.
ResNet18 seeds learned nearly the same strongest features on CIFAR-10 subsets.
Reordering neurons revealed shared first-layer features across CNN4 initializations.
CNN autoencoder seeds shared latent structure recoverable through linear maps, including distance-preserving rotations and reflections.
ResNet20 seeds learned similar features, but with different arrangements of their feature axes.
Conventional and spiking ResNet-20 networks showed high representational similarity across initializations.
Tested generative models shared parts of internal channels or nearly equivalent latent information across seeds.
BERT models fine-tuned on the same task shared cluster and global structure across seeds.
ResNet20×8 seeds shared features distributed across multiple neurons.
Similarity metrics reliably identified corresponding ResNet-18 layers across seeds.
Independently trained networks matched layers closely; one seed's representations identified corresponding representations from another.
MLPs learning trees repeatedly formed cone-shaped representations across seeds in a layer restricted to two dimensions.
Autoencoder and graph neural network representations aligned across seeds after transformations of their coordinates.
VGG seeds with factorized layers learned highly similar channel statistics after channels were aligned.
Few language-model neurons matched individually across seeds, but matched units were consistent.
Pythia models trained from different seeds shared substantial structure in their sparse-autoencoder features.
ResNet-18 seeds shared predictable principal components at every sampled layer.
Trained models aligned across seeds beyond random baselines, while ViT features showed no preferred axes.
RNN dynamics converged more across seeds with greater task demands, width, or regularization.
Multi-Object GRUs shared compact causal subspaces across seeds.
Tested networks converged to representations equivalent up to rotation across initializations.
EDLN representations provably aligned up to rotation at entropic global minima regardless of initialization.
Modular-addition models repeated the same kinds of geometric shapes across seeds despite different phase offsets.
ResNet-18 and DINO models represented concepts very similarly across seeds.
L1-penalized ReLU/Gated sparse autoencoders shared more features across seeds than TopK models retaining strongest activations.
Sparse autoencoders revealed shared features hidden by different arrangements of neurons.
Modular-addition models repeatedly learned sine-wave features, with frequencies varying across seeds.
Wider networks converged more across seeds, and some CIFAR-10 cluster neighbourhoods consistently recurred.
EMOD checkpoints shared a valence direction across seeds and training lengths.
Driving models shared deeper representations across seeds, enabling policy compatibility through linear alignment.
MNIST MLP seeds shared compact subspaces at neural collapse despite imperfect logit alignment.
Independent MLP and ResNet seeds learned neurons matchable above random baselines.
Pythia-410M seeds substantially agreed on which output-token vectors were near each other.
Models trained on the same set of tasks shared highly similar representations across seeds.
Matching revealed shared SAE features across seeds without an agreement-training loss.
A geometry-sensitive similarity measure grouped independently seeded networks by architecture and training setup.
Linear autoencoders reliably recovered shared subspaces across independent runs at larger sample sizes.
Qwen3-0.6B seeds represented waveforms similarly, despite different patterns under principal component analysis.
ResNet-18 seeds shared strong representation structure in the second-to-last layer on CIFAR datasets.
Early VGG11 channels had closely matching channels in other seeds.
Rotating representations without changing distances recovered shared content across independently initialized models.
ResNet-18 and topographic CNN (TDANN) seeds shared geometry, though matching units' spatial positions corresponded weakly.
Independent sparse autoencoders shared substantial structure recoverable by combining a few of each other's features.
TinyCNN seeds showed strongest similarity between corresponding layers.
MLP seeds shared structure tied to the task early in training, with some matching individual neurons.
ResNet-50 models' representations were more similar to each other than to those of different architectures.
Autoencoder seeds shared latent geometry recoverable through a linear map plus a shift.
Markov-chain transformers shared highly correlated core computations, though their unaligned representation subspaces barely overlapped.
Reinitialized concept-model output layers learned similarly while using the same pretrained feature-extraction network.
Rotation recovered shared features and subspaces across seeds, though direct transfer between models failed.
Skip-gram embeddings shared less representation structure across seeds than GloVe embeddings.
Middle CIFAR-10 convolutional layers varied in similarity across seeds.
Representations diverged more with memorization and clustered by learning rate.
Subspace matches reflected input or output alignment and disappeared at low output accuracy.
Shared representation subspaces matched less closely in early ConvNet layers and in ResNet18.
Dimension-reduced representations retained substantial mapping errors, while agreement in local curvature weakened toward later layers.
Disentangled models showed variable coordinate alignment across seeds and coarse shared structure on ImageNet.
Deeper differential-equation network layers retained dissimilar directions across seeds even after canonical-correlation analysis.
Similarity (CKA) on paraphrases modestly exceeded untrained-model baselines overall, but fell below them at layer 7.
CIFAR-100 seed pairs shared weaker representational structure.
Teacher-network feature recovery weakened for weakly weighted units, equally wide student networks, and higher layers.
In the Catcher game, MaxminDQN similarity across seeds fluctuated and stayed low at some training points.
Similarity measures PWCCA and Orthogonal Procrustes found weak correspondence between BERT base seeds.
Representations across seeds led to substantial downstream prediction disagreement, and many representation directions aligned weakly.
NSynth features differed more across seeds in early and late layers than middle layers.
GULP similarity tuned for fine detail exposed seed differences during training and in later BERT layers.
The study reported only moderate correlations between hidden units matched by their activations.
Connecting models' layers linearly worked worse inside residual blocks and deeper layers, reaching chance in ResNet18.
Neuron reordering left accuracy losses during merging, growing with depth, reduced width, and CNN learning rate.
Group-operation networks shared circuit types but chose different key features across seeds.
Bottleneck superposition prevented a high-accuracy recurrent network from recovering the theoretical linear circuit.
ResNet18 seeds shared weaker feature correlations when trained on only 10k examples.
Trained ResNet20 units matched less than random pairs at most tested widths.
Matching recovered limited correspondence in a large middle layer across initializations.
ResNet-20 models trained on disjoint classes showed lower activation correlations in deeper layers.
Representation similarity across seeds varied with regularization, dataset and comparison method.
Pretrained BERT seeds arranged representations differently, especially among nearby points.
Similarity measures struggled to match corresponding layers across seeds of ViT-Ti, a small vision transformer.
MultiBERT seed alignment with linear maps plus shifts varied by direction and, beyond early layers, task.
ResNet-18 alignment across seeds generally weakened when other sources of training variation were reduced.
ResNet-18 seeds shared a small subspace, but most principal components differed between seeds.
ReLU CNN seeds shared preferred neuron directions, with neuron matching sensitive to rotation.
Recurrent-network seeds retained distinct dynamics, diverging more when weights barely changed from initialization.
Universal alignment disappeared under weight balance or large weight decay in teacher-student networks.
Continuous gradient descent without noise prevented perfect alignment across initializations.
TopK sparse autoencoders shared only a minority of their learned features across seeds.
When feature overlap was low or intermediate layers had artifacts, sparse-autoencoder features aligned worse than neurons.
Across seeds, modular-addition networks learned different frequencies, and deeper transformer layers represented inputs differently.
ResNet18 seeds with similar test losses placed different clusters near each other in representation space.
Single-task models showed substantial variability in representational similarity across seeds.
Sparse-autoencoder feature correspondence remained partial across seeds and varied by task and alignment method.
Unregularized linear autoencoders shared subspaces but differed in distances and which points were close together.
Cross-model comparisons showed little advantage over within-model comparisons in MLPs and deeper VGG11 layers.
Rotating activations between models only partly matched individual features' responses in Pythia and toy models.
Penalizing connection length during training reduced representation similarity across seeds.
Sparse-autoencoder encoders matched only partly; which decoder features recurred depended strongly on the data.
Modular-addition transformers converged to cyclic operators but differed in rotational modes across seeds.
Cross-model accuracy lagged training accuracy when one concept-bottleneck run used dropout.
Intermediate VGG and ResNet layers showed little subspace matching across seeds.
From-scratch Inceptionv3 models shared information differently, although low validation accuracy complicated interpretation.

wording_issues.issue: There is no common denominator for 'many'. Highly universal PCs can be a small subset; universal-neuron thresholds count units; SAE overlap counts extracted dictionary elements; energy-profile correlations summarize spectra. These measurements cannot be exchanged for a shared-feature percentage.

wording_issues.phrase: though not the same individual units or bases
wording_issues.issue: The exclusion is too categorical. ReLU CNN rotation controls indicate partially shared preferred bases; soft matching favours native bases. MNIST MLPs have individual neurons with strong cross-seed counterparts. Other settings have weak unit matching or different bases, supporting architecture-dependent and imperfect correspondence.

Literal overlap in native coordinates differs from correspondence after alignment and from task-compatible information. Markov cores have high CCA despite low projector overlap. Under unregularized training, linear-autoencoder runs retain reliable projector agreement while failing stronger neighbor and geometric criteria. Neither low native-coordinate overlap nor failure of those stronger criteria establishes absence of V3's shared features or subspaces. Unaligned toy-transformer coordinate overlap likewise does not determine whether equivalent features recur after alignment.

Some linked results vary additional conditions: ResNet-56 comparisons change CIFAR-10 to STL-10; a ResNet-50 panel varies augmentation/training recipes; Dyck-3 Cohort A shares frozen trained input/output weights; Pythia-410M versus its deduped sibling changes training data as well as seed. These are conditional comparisons, not isolated initialization changes.

SAE initialization on a fixed language model differs from initialization of the underlying network. Shared-backbone concept bottlenecks reinitialize heads. Qwen3 compares language-pretrained and randomly initialized models without multiple seeds within each regime. The BERT joint-SAE study is ambiguous about independently initialized base models versus common-checkpoint fine-tuning.

Architecture matching alone leaves training-data and checkpoint conditions unspecified: non-target data variability changes ResNet seed similarity, and DQN agreement fluctuates across checkpoints. The linear-model results concern stronger alignment criteria. Gradient flow preserves initialization-dependent spectra and fails perfect alignment, which cannot determine whether V3's shared features or subspaces exist. Unregularized linear-autoencoder runs fail some neighbor and geometric criteria while retaining reliable projector agreement. These linear-model failures do not establish a limitation of V3.

wording_issues.phrase: learn many of the same features
wording_issues.issue: Recurring abstract structure is weaker than identifying the same concrete features. Modular-addition MLPs and transformers show recurring sinusoidal forms, while frequency selection varies across seeds; this qualifies concrete-feature convergence. In group-composition tasks, C113 Transformer seeds 2 and 4 share no key representations with the other C113 Transformer seeds, and A5 Transformer seed 4 shares none with the other A5 Transformer seeds. These conditions challenge concrete-feature recurrence; other comparisons show incomplete overlap. EMOD checkpoints align with a common external valence direction, without a direct seed-to-seed feature or subspace comparison.
The entropic-objective deep-linear theorem characterizes specified global minima. It does not establish that actual SGD reaches those minima or provide empirical seed experiments.

method_sensitivity.what: Larger-λ GULP yields smoother convergence and groups later BERT layers that small λ separates. CKA and canonical-correlation summaries give different readings in transferred-discrepancy experiments. For BERT-base seed pairs, PWCCA reports substantial dissimilarity: corresponding layer 7 is farther apart than any within-model layer comparison. CKA supports convergence, while orthogonal Procrustes shows smaller but nontrivial specificity, distinguishing layers separated by 4–5 layers. PWCCA and Procrustes indicate partial V3 convergence; their contrast with CKA demonstrates metric dependence. ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 layer identification is 12.50% with PWCCA, 19.17% with OPD, 96.11% with LCKA and 92.50% with structural direct matching.

Pythia-70m mean raw cross-seed SAE reconstruction EV spans -2.11 to 0.75 across sites and is negative internally from block 2 onward; Procrustes-aligned EV is 0.85–0.99. Failed raw transfer does not establish absent shared subspaces or recurring features. ResNet-18 CIFAR-100 feature reliability is 0.003 before alignment and 0.813 on held-out images after alignment. Myrtle CNN affine stitching recovers performance lost under permutation/scaling restrictions (arXiv:2205.14258). Separately, arXiv:2110.14633 Figure 8 reports illustrative relative accuracies: task-loss matching, 97.70% at sparsity 0.000, 91.70% at 0.837, 77.42% at 0.968; direct matching, 94.64% at 0.000, 63.64% at 0.798, 11.60% at 0.974. Increasing sparsity degrades direct matching more sharply.

Layer profiles differ: CIFAR-10 SVCCA favours initial/final over middle layers; SRM finds weaker early than final ConvNet alignment; audio CKA favours middle over early layers. Linear compatibility also depends on whether the stitch point lies inside a residual block.

Pretrained BERT topological alignment on SST2 is 0.12 at k=10 versus 0.36 at k=910; on IMDB it is 0.14 at k=10 versus 0.44 at k=1000. These indicate partial V3 convergence and observed scale dependence and incompleteness. After same-task fine-tuning, cluster-scale alignment is 0.74 on SST2 at k=910, 0.69 on IMDB at k=1000 and 0.85 on AG-News at k=500. These support V3 convergence at that scale, with weaker evidence for V7 incompleteness. IMDB fine-tuned local alignment remains 0.09 at k=10: partial V3 convergence with observed local incompleteness. Global CKA and neighbourhood agreement describe different scales.

method_sensitivity.factor: Training data, evaluation inputs and mapping direction
method_sensitivity.what: ResNet top-feature alignment increases with the larger CIFAR-10 training subset. Downstream disagreement changes with label granularity and input distribution. Random-label ConvNets agree at training softmax but fail to converge on test softmax. MultiBERT later-layer affine mapping patterns change across tasks and mapping direction.

Spatial wiring costs reduce cross-seed CKA; larger CNN learning rates leave larger post-permutation barriers; large weight decay removes tested teacher-student alignment. Catcher MaxminDQN similarity alternates between low and extremely high across training snapshots under coupled targets.

Teacher-node recovery depends on over-realization and teacher strength. Differential-equation networks become more reproducible with width, with layer-specific qualifications: at width 20, the first layer is highly reproducible and the second mostly reproducible, while the third and fourth retain about 15% dissimilar canonical components. Axis ticks do not establish individual reproducibility values across all widths and layers. Synthetic classification seed distances decline with width. RNN dynamics become less seed-dependent with larger width or stronger feature learning. Static SVCCA need not follow the dynamical trends; its qualitative account establishes metric dependence without determining factor-specific V3 convergence.

method_sensitivity.factor: Basis, SAE extraction and matching threshold
method_sensitivity.what: SAE extraction improves alignment in some toy/deep-network settings but decreases soft-matching at ResNet50 layer2.3.bn2. This establishes SAE sensitivity, without determining reversed V3 convergence or reduced shared features; the authors suggest already disentangled features and harmful SAE reconstruction artifacts. Rotation improves Pythia SAE reconstruction without identical per-feature firing. CNN native-basis rotation controls differ from ViT controls. Universal-neuron prevalence uses excess correlation after subtracting a random-basis baseline and depends on a threshold with no principled cutoff supplied by the authors.

method_sensitivity.factor: SAE fitting budget, matching flexibility and operator masking
method_sensitivity.what: Pythia 160M SAE overlap decreases with latent count and TopK k and increases with training time. On fixed Pythia-70m activations, one-to-one matching explains a fraction 0.22 of whole-operator energy versus 0.57 with sparse maps; masked transport explains 0.47. The reported 0.85 concerns a source coactive block carrying the unmasked target operator, not whole-operator recovery. For SST-2 BERT extraction without cross-code loss, top-100 correlation is 0.220 without rotation and 0.432 with rotation; universality remains 12.7±9.1% among active-in-both features.

Function-preserving ReLU rescaling changes raw weight dissimilarity, while CKA preserves the within-dataset versus between-dataset separation. The latter demonstrates robustness of broad grouping. Autoencoder translation depends on normalization and transformation class. Relative-representation distances change when cosine similarity is replaced by vector-quantized similarity and its threshold varies. LFM depends on descriptors, anchor count, graph distance and spectral dimension.

status_amendment.public_note: The explanation now includes two more challenges: English BERT models trained from different random starts matched each other less than a random control did at one layer, when compared on paraphrased sentences, and some small transformers trained on group operations shared none of their key features with other transformer runs on the same task. The level is unchanged at C (contested).
